tips: Say «لا أعرف... هيا نبحث معًا» ("I don't know, let's find out together").
Praise the question, not the answer.

mysteries.find: Make a rainbow with a glass of water in sunlight

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- Sunlight looks white, but it is really all the colours mixed together.
  - When sunlight shines into raindrops, it bends going in, bounces off the back of each drop and bends again coming out.
    Each colour bends a slightly different amount, so the colours spread apart: red on the outside, violet on the inside.
  - You only see a rainbow with the sun behind you and the rain in front, usually in the morning or late afternoon.
  - A surprise for her "end of the rainbow" hint: a rainbow has no end. It is really a full circle; the ground hides the
    bottom half. From an aeroplane, people sometimes see the whole circle.
  - Each person sees their own rainbow, from their own drops.
  - In the desert, rain is rare, so a desert rainbow is special.

card.label: Find out together
card.md:
- On a sunny morning or late afternoon, fill a clear glass to the top and stand it in direct sun on a windowsill or
    table.
  - Hold a sheet of white paper near it and move the paper until the colours appear.
  - Another way: spray a hose into the air with your backs to the sun.

card.label: Safety
card.md:
- Never look straight at the sun.
  - Use a sturdy glass, placed safely, and wipe up spills.

mysteries.find: Mix paints and make her own colour chart

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- Paint gets its colour by soaking up some colours of light and bouncing back the rest.
  - Yellow paint bounces back mostly yellow and a little green. Blue paint bounces back mostly blue and a little green.
    Mixed together, each soaks up what the other bounces back, and the colour they both still bounce back is green.
  - White makes a colour lighter (red and white make pink). A tiny bit of black makes it darker.
  - With red, yellow and blue (plus white), she can mix a huge number of colours.
  - Coloured light mixes differently from paint: on a screen, red and green light make yellow. That is another mystery
    for later.

card.label: Find out together
card.md: mix paints and make her own colour chart: which two colours made each new one?

card.label: Safety
card.md: washable children's paint, an apron, and a covered table.

mysteries.find: What flamingos eat and why it turns them pink

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- Flamingo chicks hatch grey or white. They turn pink because of natural colours in their food: tiny shrimps and algae
    (very small water plants).
  - Their bodies turn these colours into pink and red in their feathers, skin and legs. It takes a young flamingo about
    two to three years to become fully pink.
  - In zoos, flamingos get special food with the same colours, or they slowly fade.
  - The same family of natural colours makes carrots orange.
  - Her hint asks about green food: a flamingo would not turn green. Without its pink-making food, its new feathers
    simply grow paler.
  - Greater flamingos spend the winter on Saudi Arabia's coasts.

card.label: Find out together
card.md: find out what flamingos eat and how they eat it (upside down, with their heads in the water).

card.label: Safety
card.md: none.

mysteries.find: Draw an eight-pointed star with a compass and ruler

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- Islamic geometric patterns are built from circles and straight lines. The craftsmen used only a compass and a
    straight edge.
  - Dividing a circle into equal parts gives stars with 8, 10, 12 or more points.
  - An eight-pointed star is two squares of the same size on top of each other, one turned like a diamond.
  - In tile mosaics, each small piece is cut by hand and fitted with others so that the pattern repeats and covers the
    whole wall with no gaps. Such patterns decorate mosques and palaces from Spain to Central Asia, and in Algeria too,
    for example in Tlemcen.

card.label: Find out together
card.md:
draw an eight-pointed star together: draw a circle, a square inside it, then a second square
  turned like a diamond.

card.label: Safety
card.md: the compass point is sharp, so an adult stays close.

mysteries.find: Family asks her questions about her drawing; she answers

card.label: Why this one first
card.md:
she knows more about this picture than anyone in the world. There is nothing to get wrong, so
  her first storm feels safe. It also lets her practise explaining her choices aloud.

card.label: Find out together
card.md:
- The family asks her questions about her drawing, and she answers.
  - Ask open questions, for example why she chose a colour, or what would change at night. Wait quietly for her answer.
  - Show real interest.
  - This is also modelling: she hears what good questions sound like.

card.label: Safety
card.md: none.

mysteries.find: Hand shadows on a wall in afternoon sunlight
Henna leaves, and why the colour deepens over a day

mysteries.line: كلّ ألوان الشاشة من ثلاثة ألوان فقط
mysteries.find: Look at a screen through a magnifying glass
Make one with salt coloured with chalk
Put one squishy in the fridge for an hour, compare with another

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- A squishy is made of a special slow-rising foam, full of tiny air pockets.
  - When she presses it, the air is pushed out. It rises slowly because air can only seep back in through very tiny holes,
    and because the foam itself is made to move slowly.
  - Cold makes the foam stiffer, so it rises even more slowly. Warmth makes it softer and quicker.
  - The foam is a cousin of memory foam, which was developed for NASA in the 1960s to make aeroplane seats safer: a link
    to her love of space.

card.label: Find out together
card.md:
- Put one squishy in the fridge for an hour and keep a matching one in the room.
  - Press both together, then count or time how long each takes to rise.
  - She predicts first.

card.label: Safety
card.md:
- Use a squishy she does not mind changing.
  - The fridge is fine. If you also try the sun, keep it short (about 10 minutes), because strong sun can fade and crack
    foam.
  - Never use the microwave or oven.
  - Squishies are not for biting or chewing.

mysteries.find: Shine a torch on sequins and on plain fabric

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- Sequins are tiny, flat, shiny discs, today usually plastic with a thin metal-like coating.
  - A smooth, shiny surface bounces light back in one direction, like a mirror. When that light comes straight into her
    eyes, she sees a flash.
  - Plain fabric is made of rough little threads that scatter light in every direction, so it looks soft, not shiny.
  - Every sequin sits at a slightly different angle, so as she moves, different sequins flash: that is the sparkle.
  - Each sequin has a tiny hole and is sewn on with a needle and thread. Today machines do most of it.
  - People have sewn shiny discs onto clothes for thousands of years: gold ones were found on clothes in Tutankhamun's
    tomb in Egypt.
  - A surprise: the English word "sequin" comes from the Arabic سكّة, the stamp used to make coins, through an old
    Italian gold coin.

card.label: Find out together
card.md: shine a torch on sequins and on plain fabric in a dim room, and move it slowly.

card.label: Safety
card.md: never shine the torch into anyone's eyes. Needles only with an adult.

mysteries.find: Sunscreen on clear plastic over coloured paper in the sun for a few days
mysteries.homeTip: your own face cream and a sunscreen tube

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- Sunlight carries invisible rays called ultraviolet (UV). Too much UV burns the skin, and over many years it harms it.
  - Sunscreen puts a very thin shield on the skin. Some sunscreens soak up the UV rays, and others bounce them away.
  - The SPF number on the tube tells how well it protects against burning.
  - It works best put on about 15 minutes before going out, and again every two hours, or after swimming or sweating.

card.label: Find out together
card.md:
- Spread sunscreen on one half of a clear plastic sheet (a plastic sleeve works) and lay it over coloured paper in a
    sunny window for a few days.
  - Which half of the paper fades?

card.label: Safety
card.md: the paper stays in the sun, not Maria. Keep cream out of eyes, and use a children's sunscreen on her skin.

mysteries.find: Look at a zip with a magnifying glass

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- A zip has two rows of tiny teeth. Each tooth has a little bump on top and a hollow underneath.
  - The slider is shaped like a Y. Moving up, it pushes the two rows together at an angle, so each bump hooks into the
    hollow of the tooth on the other side. Moving down, a little wedge inside pushes them apart.
  - An American inventor, Whitcomb Judson, made an early version in 1893. A Swedish-American engineer, Gideon Sundback,
    designed the zip we use today between 1913 and 1917.
  - Her hint about a broken tooth: the teeth cannot lock at that spot, so the zip splits open there.

card.label: Find out together
card.md: look at a zip with a magnifying glass, then open and close it very slowly.

card.label: Safety
card.md: mind fingers and hair in zips.

mysteries.line: لاصقٌ صُنع بعد نزهةٍ مع كلب
mysteries.find: The story of Velcro and burdock seeds

mysteries.line: قطرات ماءٍ على كأسٍ بارد من الخارج
mysteries.find: Cold glass on the table, dry it, watch drops return
Taste different stages; ask at the market
Spray in one corner; each person raises a hand when they smell it
Watch a slow-motion video

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- Inside a cat's ears is a balance sense that always knows which way is down.
  - When it falls, it turns its head first. Then it twists its front half, with its front legs tucked in, and then its
    back half. A very bendy back and a loose collarbone make this possible.
  - It then spreads out a little and lands softly, with bent legs.
  - Kittens learn to do this at about three to four weeks old.
  - A surprise: the tail is not the secret. Cats born without tails can do it too.
  - Cats can still be badly hurt in falls, especially from balconies and windows.

card.label: Find out together
card.md:
watch a slow-motion video of a cat landing (you search for it, in the parent area or on your
  phone).

card.label: Safety
card.md: never drop, throw or push a cat, or any animal, to see what happens.

mysteries.find: Why chameleons really change colour

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- Many people think chameleons change colour to match what they sit on and hide. In fact, they mainly change colour to
    show how they feel and to "talk" to other chameleons (calm, angry, scared, or showing off). They also change to
    control their warmth: darker to soak up sunshine when cool, paler when hot.
  - How: under the outer skin is a layer of cells packed with tiny crystals. When the chameleon relaxes or gets excited,
    the crystals move closer together or further apart, and this changes which colours of light bounce back. Other cells
    add yellow, red and dark colours.
  - A surprise for her "what if on coloured paper" hint: it would not turn the colour of the paper. Its usual colours
    already suit leaves and branches.
  - Saudi Arabia has its own chameleons, mostly in the green south-west.

card.label: Find out together
card.md:
- Find out why chameleons really change colour.
  - Look at photos of the same chameleon calm and excited, or watch a short wildlife film together.

card.label: Safety
card.md: do not catch or handle wild chameleons or lizards; it frightens them. In a pet shop, just look.

mysteries.find: How far she can turn her own head

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- An owl's eyes are very large and shaped like tubes, fixed in place. It cannot roll its eyes as we do, so it turns
    its whole head instead.
  - It can turn its head about 270 degrees, three quarters of the way round (not a full circle).
  - Its neck has 14 bones, twice as many as ours (we have 7), which makes it very bendy.
  - Special blood vessels keep blood flowing to its brain even while its neck is twisted.

card.label: Find out together
card.md:
how far can she turn her own head? Ask her to look over her shoulder slowly while you watch.
  People manage about a quarter of the way round each side.

card.label: Safety
card.md: turn slowly and gently, never with a jerk.

mysteries.find: The fennec, Algeria's national animal

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- The fennec is the smallest fox in the world, about the size of a small cat, and its ears can be about 15 centimetres
    long.
  - The big ears help in two ways. They let heat escape, which keeps it cool in the desert. And they hear tiny sounds,
    even insects moving under the sand, so it can dig them out.
  - Thick fur on the soles of its feet protects them from the hot sand.
  - It lives in the Sahara, including Algeria. It sleeps in a burrow in the heat of the day and comes out at night.
  - It is Algeria's national animal, and Algeria's football team is nicknamed "Les Fennecs".

card.label: Find out together
card.md: find out more about the fennec, Algeria's national animal: what it eats, and where it sleeps.

card.label: Safety
card.md: fennecs are wild animals, not pets.

mysteries.credit: Wikimedia Commons, Anass ERRIHANI, CC BY-SA 4.0

mysteries.find: How the oryx was brought back

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- The Arabian oryx was hunted until it disappeared from the wild. The last wild ones were shot in 1972.
  - Luckily, a few lived in zoos. They had babies, and their young were brought back to the desert from 1982, in Oman,
    then in Saudi Arabia (from 1990), Jordan and the Emirates, in protected reserves.
  - In 2011 it became the first animal ever to go from "extinct in the wild" back to "vulnerable".
  - It eats grasses, leaves and roots, and gets much of its water from plants and dew, so it can go for weeks without
    drinking. Its white coat reflects the sun.

card.label: Find out together
card.md: find out how the oryx was brought back, and look at photos of a reserve.

card.label: Safety
card.md: none.

mysteries.find: Watch a waggle-dance video
How many hen's eggs fit in one
Links to her school life-cycle lesson
Falconry in Saudi heritage
Draw the moon each evening for a week; link to the Hijri months

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- The moon does not really change shape. The sun always lights half of it.
  - As the moon travels around the Earth (about once every 29 and a half days), we see more or less of that lit half:
    crescent, half, full, and back again.
  - The Hijri month begins when the new thin crescent (الهلال) is seen. The full moon (البدر) comes around the middle of
    the month.
  - Her hint about the sea: the moon's pull makes most of the sea's tides, the rise and fall of the water at the coast.
    Without the moon, tides would be much smaller.

card.label: Find out together
card.md:
- Draw the moon each evening for a week, with the Hijri date under each drawing.
  - In a dark room, shine a torch on a ball while she turns slowly, holding it at arm's length.

card.label: Safety
card.md: none (looking at the moon is safe).

mysteries.line: الماء يطفو كرةً في محطة الفضاء
mysteries.find: Astronaut drinking video

mysteries.line: ريّانة برناوي أوّل رائدة فضاء سعودية
mysteries.find: Her 2023 mission and what she studied
Photos from the Mars rovers

mysteries.line: في الصحراء نرى نجومًا أكثر من المدينة
mysteries.find: Stargazing on a family desert trip

mysteries.line: ضوء الشمس يحتاج ثماني دقائق ليصل إلينا
mysteries.find: How fast light travels
Saturn photos
She explains her concept and colours to the family

card.label: Why this one
card.md: her own idea again, so the storm stays safe while the topic moves to space.

card.label: Find out together
card.md:
she explains her concept and her colours to the family. Real answers in case she asks:
  - Rockets carry spacecraft into space. A trip to the Moon takes about three days, and a trip to Mars takes about
    seven months.
  - Scientists have not found living things on any other planet yet. They are still looking, for example with robots on
    Mars that search for signs of tiny life from long ago.
  - If she asks something you do not know, say «لا أعرف... هيا نبحث معًا».

card.label: Safety
card.md: none.

mysteries.find: Ink fingerprints of the whole family; compare with a magnifier

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- Fingerprints are the tiny ridges on our fingertips.
  - They form before birth, from about the 10th week of pregnancy, and are set by about the 17th week.
  - Genes play a part, and so do tiny differences in how each baby lies and grows in the womb. This is why even identical
    twins have different fingerprints.
  - The pattern stays the same all her life; it just grows bigger as she grows. The three main patterns are loops (the
    most common), whorls and arches.
  - What they are for: scientists are still not completely sure. They probably help us feel textures, and may help us
    grip rough or wet things. A good moment for «لا أعرف... هيا نبحث معًا».
  - A surprise for an animal lover: koalas have fingerprints very like ours.

card.label: Find out together
card.md:
- Make ink fingerprints of the whole family and compare them with a magnifying glass.
  - Find who has loops, whorls or arches.
  - No ink at home? Shade a dark patch with a soft pencil, press a fingertip on it, then press clear sticky tape on the
    finger and stick the tape on white paper.

card.label: Safety
card.md: use washable, non-toxic ink only, and wash hands afterwards.

mysteries.line: التثاؤب ينتقل من شخصٍ إلى آخر
mysteries.find: Try yawning at dinner and count who catches it

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- Scientists are still not sure exactly why we yawn. One idea is that it helps cool the brain and wake us up when we
    are tired or bored.
  - Seeing, hearing, or even reading about a yawn can make us yawn. We catch yawns more easily from family and friends.
  - Children usually start catching yawns at about four or five years old.
  - Her hint about animals: some studies found that dogs can catch yawns from people, especially their owners.
    Chimpanzees catch yawns too. Nobody really knows about cats: a lovely one to wonder about.

card.label: Find out together
card.md: yawn at dinner and count who catches it.

card.label: Safety
card.md: none.

mysteries.find: Test after a bath; why it might help grip
mysteries.homeTip: her wrinkly fingers after a bath

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- After about five to ten minutes in water, fingers and toes wrinkle. It happens faster in warm water.
  - It is not only the skin soaking up water. The nerves tell the tiny blood vessels under the skin to narrow, the soft
    fingertip shrinks a little, and the skin on top folds into wrinkles.
  - Scientists think the wrinkles may help us grip wet things, a bit like the pattern on a tyre. Not every study agrees,
    so it is still being explored.
  - The wrinkles go away within about half an hour after drying.
  - It only happens on the fingers and toes, the palms and the soles of the feet.

card.label: Find out together
card.md:
- Test after a bath: are her toes wrinkly too?
  - Move wet marbles or pebbles from one bowl to another, once with dry fingers and once with wrinkly ones. Which is
    easier?

card.label: Safety
card.md: warm water, not hot. Keep marbles away from little ones (they can choke).

mysteries.find: Count her pulse before and after 30 seconds of jumping

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- The heart is a muscle about the size of her fist.
  - When she jumps, her muscles need more oxygen from the blood. So her heart beats faster and harder, and she breathes
    faster too.
  - When she rests, it slows down again within a few minutes.
  - At rest, a child her age usually has roughly 70 to 110 beats a minute. After jumping it climbs much higher.

card.label: Find out together
card.md:
- Count her pulse before and after 30 seconds of jumping.
  - To find it, put two fingers (not the thumb, which has its own pulse) on the inside of her wrist, below the thumb.
    Or press gently on one side of her neck.
  - Count for 15 seconds and multiply by 4. You can do the sum together.
  - She can also put her hand on her chest after jumping and feel it.

card.label: Safety
card.md:
- Jump on a clear, non-slippery floor, away from furniture, in bare feet or trainers (not socks on tiles).
  - Stop if she feels dizzy or unwell.
  - Press gently on the neck, on one side only.

mysteries.line: حين أسُدّ أنفي لا أعرف طعم التفاحة
mysteries.find: Blindfold taste test, nose pinched

mysteries.line: في يدي أكثر من خمس وعشرين عظمة
mysteries.find: Count finger joints together
Count teeth in the mirror
Watch her pupils in a mirror near a lamp

mysteries.line: حفّاضةٌ تشرب الماء ولا يخرج منها!
mysteries.what: A clean nappy drinks a whole cup of water and gets heavy; the crystals inside turn into jelly
mysteries.predictEn: How many cups of water will the nappy drink?
mysteries.homeTip: a clean nappy with a cup of water beside it

card.label: What happens
card.md:
the nappy drinks cup after cup, gets heavy, and the water does not run back out, even when it is
  squeezed a little.

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- Inside a nappy is a fluffy layer mixed with tiny white crystals of a special "super-soaking" material.
  - Each crystal can soak up many, many times its own weight in water. The water goes inside the crystals and turns
    them into soft jelly.
  - Her question, why the wee does not come out: the liquid is locked inside the jelly, so it cannot flow back out. The
    top layer lets liquid pass through quickly, so the side next to the baby feels drier.
  - Her question, why it gets heavy: the water is still there, only trapped. Water is heavy: one cup weighs about a
    quarter of a kilo.
  - A surprise for the salt hint: sprinkle salt on the jelly and it turns runny again, because salt makes the crystals
    let go of the water. That is also why a nappy holds less wee than plain water: wee is a little salty.

card.label: Find out together
card.md:
- She predicts how many cups. Then pour water onto a clean new nappy one cup at a time, and count until it cannot take
    any more.
  - Weigh the nappy dry and again full, on a kitchen scale.
  - You cut open a second, dry nappy over a tray and shake out the crystals. Add water to a spoonful and watch the jelly
    grow, then sprinkle salt on it.

card.label: Safety
card.md:
- Only an adult cuts the nappy, over a tray.
  - Do not breathe in the powder, and keep it away from eyes and mouths. Wash hands afterwards.
  - Put the jelly in the bin, never down the sink (it can block the drain).

mysteries.predict: كم كوبًا من الماء ستشرب الحفّاضة؟

mysteries.what: Pepper flees from a soapy finger
mysteries.predictEn: What will the pepper do when she touches it?
mysteries.homeTip: pepper sprinkled on water in a white plate

card.label: What happens
card.md: the pepper rushes away to the edges of the plate.

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- The top of water behaves like a thin, stretched skin, because water particles pull on each other. Pepper is so
    light that it rests on that skin.
  - Soap weakens the pull where it touches. The stronger pull of the water further away drags the surface outwards, and
    the pepper rides along with it.
  - The pepper is not "afraid" of the soap: it is carried by the water's surface.
  - A clean finger does almost nothing. Try that first, so she can compare.

card.label: Find out together
card.md:
- First touch the middle with a clean, dry finger, then with a finger dipped in washing-up liquid.
  - Her hint asks about sugar and salt: try a pinch of each in a fresh plate of pepper water and see what happens.

card.label: Safety
card.md:
- Keep pepper away from eyes and noses (it stings and makes you sneeze).
  - Use a little washing-up liquid on the finger only, and wash hands afterwards. Nothing is for drinking.

mysteries.predict: ماذا سيفعل الفلفل حين نلمس الماء بإصبعٍ عليه صابون؟

mysteries.what: Coloured water climbs paper towels between cups
mysteries.predictEn: What will the middle cup look like tomorrow?
mysteries.homeTip: the cups and paper-towel strips, set up

card.label: What happens
card.md:
the coloured water climbs up the paper, over the top and down into the empty middle cup. Yellow and
  blue make the middle cup green.

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- A paper towel is made of tiny fibres with tiny gaps between them.
  - Water clings to the fibres and pulls more water along behind it, so it can climb up the gaps against gravity. This
    is called capillary action. Plants use the same pull to lift water up their stems.
  - The water stops moving when the cups are about equally full.

card.label: Find out together
card.md:
- Three cups in a row: yellow water on one side, blue on the other, the middle one empty. A folded strip of paper
    towel bridges each pair of cups.
  - She predicts, then you look again after an hour and the next morning.

card.label: Safety
card.md: food colouring stains, so cover the table and use plastic cups. An adult adds the colouring.

mysteries.what: Egg sinks, then floats after salt is added
mysteries.predictEn: Will the egg float? And with salt?
mysteries.homeTip: an egg in a glass of water

card.label: What happens
card.md: the egg sinks in plain water. After enough salt is stirred in, it floats.

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- A fresh egg is a little heavier than the same amount of plain water, so it sinks.
  - Salt dissolved in the water makes the water heavier for its size. When the water becomes heavier than the egg, the
    egg floats.
  - This is why it is easier to float in the sea than in a swimming pool, and why people float so easily in the very
    salty Dead Sea.
  - A surprise: an old egg can float even in plain water, because air collects inside it as it ages.

card.label: Find out together
card.md:
- Plain water first, after her prediction. Then add salt one spoon at a time, stirring each in, and count the spoons:
    it usually takes several.
  - Her hint asks about sugar: try it in a second glass.

card.label: Safety
card.md: a raw egg, so wash hands afterwards. Use a sturdy glass. The salty water is not for drinking.

mysteries.predict: هل ستطفو البيضة؟ وإذا أضفنا الملح؟

mysteries.what: Salt lets a string stick to ice
mysteries.predictEn: Can a string lift an ice cube?

mysteries.what: Food colouring swirls when soap touches milk
A pencil looks broken in water

mysteries.find: Camel eyelashes, nostrils, feet and hump

verse.text: أَفَلَا يَنظُرُونَ إِلَى ٱلْإِبِلِ كَيْفَ خُلِقَتْ

card.label: Respect
card.md:
the verse invites us to look and reflect. Share the facts below as things to wonder at, without linking
  the verse to any scientific claim. Let her questions lead.

card.label: Explanation (things to wonder at)
card.md:
- **The hump** stores fat, not water. The camel's body can use it for energy when food is scarce. When the fat is used
    up, the hump becomes smaller and floppy.
  - **Thirst:** a camel saves water in many ways. Its body warms up by several degrees during the day before it starts to
    sweat, and it loses very little water in its droppings.
    - In summer heat it can go about a week or more without a drink, and much longer in cooler months, when it eats green
      plants.
    - When it does drink, a very thirsty camel can take in around 100 litres in about ten minutes.
  - **Eyes:** two rows of long eyelashes, and a thin third eyelid that wipes sand away. It can also close its nostrils in
    a sandstorm.
  - **Feet:** two toes on a wide, leathery pad that spreads out on sand, so it does not sink. Tough pads on its chest and
    knees let it kneel on hot sand.

card.label: Find out together
card.md:
- Look at close-up photos of camel eyelashes, nostrils, feet and the hump.
  - If you pass camels on a drive, stop and watch them together.
  - Press a flat hand, then one finger, into sand or flour: which one sinks?

card.label: Safety
card.md: watch real camels only from a safe distance, with an adult. Camels can kick and bite.

mysteries.find: Watch clouds change for ten minutes

card.label: Respect
card.md:
the verse invites us to look and reflect. Share the facts below as things to wonder at, without linking
  the verse to any scientific claim. Let her questions lead.

card.label: Explanation (things to wonder at)
card.md:
- **Blue:** sunlight looks white, but it is all the colours mixed. The air scatters blue light much more than red, all
    over the sky, so blue reaches our eyes from every direction.
  - **Sunset:** the light crosses much more air, the blue is scattered away on the journey, and the reds and oranges
    are left.
  - **Clouds:** they are made of tiny water droplets or bits of ice, so small and light that rising air holds them up.
    When droplets join into bigger drops, they fall as rain.
  - **Above the clouds:** big aeroplanes fly about 10 to 12 kilometres up, often above most of the clouds, where the sky
    is a deeper blue.

card.label: Find out together
card.md:
lie on a blanket or sit by a window and watch the clouds change for ten minutes. What shapes
  does she see?

card.label: Safety
card.md: never look straight at the sun.

mysteries.find: Layers in rocks; a family trip photo

card.label: Respect
card.md:
the verse invites us to look and reflect. Share the facts below as things to wonder at, without linking
  the verse to any scientific claim. Let her questions lead.

card.label: Explanation (things to wonder at)
card.md:
- Most mountains form very slowly, over millions of years, when huge pieces of the Earth's outer shell push together
    and fold and lift the rock up. Some, like volcanoes, are built from melted rock coming out.
  - Wind, rain and ice wear mountains down very slowly.
  - The Sarawat mountains (السروات) run down the west of Saudi Arabia, near the Red Sea. The highest peaks, in the
    south-west near Abha, reach about 3,000 metres.
  - Some rocks in the mountains of western Saudi Arabia are more than 600 million years old.
  - Many rocks form in layers, from sand and mud pressed down over a very long time. That is why some cliffs have
    stripes.

card.label: Find out together
card.md: look for layers in rocks and cliffs, in photos or on a family trip, and take a photo.

card.label: Safety
card.md: on a trip, stay away from cliff edges and loose rocks, with an adult.

mysteries.credit: Wikimedia Commons, Richard Mortel, CC BY 2.0

mysteries.find: Look at the horizon from a high place

card.label: Respect
card.md:
the verse invites us to look and reflect. Share the facts below as things to wonder at, without linking
  the verse to any scientific claim. Let her questions lead.

card.label: Explanation (things to wonder at)
card.md:
- The Earth is a huge ball, so big that the part we stand on looks flat and spread out to us.
  - The horizon is where the Earth's curve hides what lies beyond. On flat ground it is only about 5 kilometres away for
    an adult. From a high place we can see much further.
  - Under the sand are layers of rock. In many places deep under Saudi Arabia, water is stored inside the rock, from rain
    that fell long ago.

card.label: Find out together
card.md:
look at the horizon from a high place (a roof, a hill or a tall building) and compare it with
  the view from the ground.

card.label: Safety
card.md: high places only with an adult, well away from the edge.

mysteries.find: Draw hexagons; why bees use them

mysteries.line: ﴿قَالَتْ نَمْلَةٌ يَا أَيُّهَا النَّمْلُ ادْخُلُوا مَسَاكِنَكُمْ﴾ (النمل: 18)
mysteries.find: Watch ants with a crumb of sugar

verse.text: قَالَتْ نَمْلَةٌ يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّمْلُ ٱدْخُلُوا۟ مَسَـٰكِنَكُمْ

mysteries.bankLine: ﴿قَالَتْ نَمْلَةٌ يَا أَيُّهَا النَّمْلُ ادْخُلُوا مَسَاكِنَكُمْ﴾ (النمل: 18)

mysteries.find: Plant a seed and watch it after watering

mysteries.line: ﴿أَلَمْ تَرَ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ كَيْفَ مَدَّ الظِّلَّ﴾ (الفرقان: 45)
mysteries.find: Mark a stick's shadow at three times of day

verse.text: أَلَمْ تَرَ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ كَيْفَ مَدَّ ٱلظِّلَّ

mysteries.bankLine: ﴿أَلَمْ تَرَ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ كَيْفَ مَدَّ الظِّلَّ﴾ (الفرقان: 45)

mysteries.find: Listen to whale songs together

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- Male humpback whales sing long songs that repeat, mostly in the season when they look for a mate. Scientists think
    the songs help with that and with keeping in touch, but they still do not know exactly what the songs mean. A good
    moment for «لا أعرف... هيا نبحث معًا».
  - All the males in one part of the ocean sing the same song, and it slowly changes over the months, as if they learn
    it from each other.
  - Sound travels about four times faster in water than in air, and much further: low whale sounds can be heard many
    kilometres away.
  - Whales have no ears sticking out. They hear through their heads and jaws.
  - A mother and her calf make very soft sounds to each other, almost a whisper, so that other animals do not hear.

card.label: Find out together
card.md: listen to more whale songs together and talk about what they sound like.

card.label: Safety
card.md: keep the volume gentle.

mysteries.credit: Wikimedia Commons, National Marine Sanctuaries, Public domain

mysteries.line: صوتي في التسجيل يختلف عن صوتي في رأسي
mysteries.find: Speak with ears covered, then uncovered

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- When she speaks, she hears her voice in two ways: through the air into her ears, like everyone else, and through
    the bones of her head, which carry the low, deep sounds.
  - So inside her head her voice sounds deeper and fuller. A recording has only the air part, so it sounds higher to
    her. But the recording is how everyone else hears her.
  - Almost everyone is surprised by their own recorded voice at first. Her voice is lovely.
  - Her hint about an echo: sound bounces off a far, hard surface like a cliff and comes back to us a moment later.

card.label: Find out together
card.md: she talks or hums with her ears covered, then uncovered. When does her voice sound louder?

card.label: Safety
card.md: cover the ears gently; never press hard.

mysteries.find: Turn the pot and watch it lean back over a few days

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- Plants make their own food from light, air and water, so light matters to them.
  - A plant substance gathers on the shady side of the stem and makes the cells there grow longer. The longer side
    pushes the stem over, so it bends towards the light.
  - If the pot is turned round, the plant bends back towards the light within a few days.

card.label: Find out together
card.md: turn the pot and watch it lean back over a few days. Take a photo each day.

card.label: Safety
card.md: none.

mysteries.find: Water both for a week (she predicts first)
mysteries.homeTip: a pebble and a bean in two cups of damp cotton

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- A seed is alive. Inside it is a tiny baby plant and a store of food. With water, air and warmth it wakes up and
    starts to grow: first a root, then a shoot.
  - A pebble is not alive. It cannot grow, take in food, or make new pebbles.
  - A bean on damp cotton usually sprouts within about three to seven days.
  - Her hint about more water: a seed covered in water cannot get air, so it may not grow. Damp is better than soaked.

card.label: Find out together
card.md: water both cups a little each day for a week. She predicts first.

card.label: Safety
card.md: dry kitchen beans are for planting only, never for eating raw. Wash hands afterwards.

mysteries.find: Look with a magnifier or a phone zoom

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- All living things are made of tiny building blocks called cells.
  - In onion skin, the cells look like little boxes side by side. Plant cells have stiff walls, which give them that
    shape.
  - One onion skin has thousands of cells. Her own body has trillions.
  - Onion cells are too small to see clearly by eye. A strong magnifier or a phone's zoom may show a faint pattern; a
    toy microscope shows them clearly.

card.label: Find out together
card.md:
you peel a very thin, see-through layer from inside an onion, and she looks with a magnifier or
  a phone zoom.

card.label: Safety
card.md: only an adult uses the knife.

mysteries.find: Count the seeds; plant one

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- A pomegranate usually holds several hundred seeds. Each juicy red jewel has one seed inside.
  - Plants make many seeds because most will never grow: they are eaten, or land in a bad place.
  - Birds and other animals eat the fruit and drop the seeds somewhere else. That is how seeds travel far from the
    plant.
  - A pomegranate seed planted in soil can grow into a new tree, but it takes a few years to give fruit.

card.label: Find out together
card.md: count the seeds together in groups of ten, then plant one or two in a pot.

card.label: Safety
card.md: the juice stains, so use an apron or old clothes. An adult cuts the fruit.

mysteries.find: Time-lapse video of a tadpole

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- A frog starts as an egg in the water. A tadpole hatches, with a tail for swimming and gills for breathing in water.
  - Back legs grow first, then front legs. Lungs grow, so it can breathe air.
  - Her hint about the tail: it does not fall off. The body slowly takes it back in and uses it as food for growing.
  - For many frogs the whole change takes about three months.

card.label: Find out together
card.md: watch a time-lapse video of a tadpole changing.

card.label: Safety
card.md: if you see tadpoles in a pond, just look. Wash hands after touching pond water.

mysteries.find: Look at pollen on a flower with a magnifier

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- The yellow dust is pollen, made by flowers. Bees collect it, with sweet nectar, as food for their hive.
  - Pollen sticks to the bee's fuzzy hairs. When the bee visits the next flower, some rubs off, and the flower can then
    make seeds and fruit.
  - Many fruits and vegetables need bees and other insects to carry their pollen. Without them we would have far fewer
    apples, almonds and melons.

card.label: Find out together
card.md: look at the pollen inside a flower with a magnifier (a lily or a sunflower shows it well).

card.label: Safety
card.md: watch bees from a distance and never touch them. Pollen stains clothes and can make some people sneeze.

mysteries.credit: Wikimedia Commons, Clinton & Charles Robertson from RAF Lakenheath, UK & San Marcos, TX, USA & UK, CC BY-SA 2.0

mysteries.find: Touch (carefully) and compare a cactus with a leafy plant

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- A cactus's spines are its leaves, changed into thin, hard points. Flat leaves would lose a lot of water in the
    desert heat, and spines lose almost none.
  - Its thick green stem stores water and makes the plant's food, the job leaves do in other plants. A waxy skin keeps
    the water in.
  - The spines also protect it from thirsty animals and give it a little shade.
  - Its roots spread wide just under the ground, to soak up rain quickly when it comes.

card.label: Find out together
card.md:
compare a cactus with a leafy plant: feel the leafy plant's leaves, and look closely at the
  cactus's thick stem and spines.

card.label: Safety
card.md: spines prick. An adult shows where to touch (a smooth part of the stem, gently, or not at all).

mysteries.credit: Wikimedia Commons, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Public domain

mysteries.find: Find hidden animals in camouflage photos

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- A stick insect looks just like a twig: long, thin and brown or green. It even sways gently, like a branch in the
    wind.
  - It keeps still in the day and eats leaves at night.
  - Birds and lizards hunt by looking, so looking like a stick keeps it safe. This is called camouflage.

card.label: Find out together
card.md: find the hidden animals in camouflage photos (owls on bark, leaf insects, crabs on sand).

card.label: Safety
card.md: none.

mysteries.credit: Wikimedia Commons, gbohne from Berlin, Germany, CC BY-SA 2.0

mysteries.find: Two apple slices in closed jars, one in the fridge (predict first; never open the mouldy jar)

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- A cut apple turns brown within minutes because the air reacts with it. That is not mould.
  - Over days, tiny living things (moulds and bacteria) start to feed on the old fruit and break it down.
  - This is nature's recycling: what is left goes back into the soil and feeds new plants.
  - Cold slows these tiny living things down, so food in the fridge lasts longer.

card.label: Find out together
card.md:
put two apple slices in two closed jars, one in the fridge and one on a shelf. She predicts
  first, then you look each day through the glass.

card.label: Safety
card.md: keep the jars closed. Never open, smell or touch the mouldy one; an adult throws it away, jar and all.

mysteries.find: Start a family recycling box and count cans for a month

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- Drinks cans are made of aluminium. At the recycling plant they are shredded, melted and rolled into new sheets, for
    new cans or other things, such as bicycle frames.
  - Recycling aluminium uses about 95 per cent less energy than making new aluminium from rock.
  - A can can be recycled again and again without getting worse. A bicycle frame takes hundreds of cans.
  - Her hint about throwing a can on the sand: a can does not rot away. It can lie there for a very long time, until
    someone picks it up.

card.label: Find out together
card.md: start a family recycling box and count the cans for a month.

card.label: Safety
card.md: rinse the cans. Torn cans have sharp edges, so an adult handles any damaged ones.

mysteries.credit: Wikimedia Commons, Ruth Hartnup from Vancouver, Canada, CC BY 2.0

mysteries.find: How Saudi Arabia protects the leopard and the oryx (C5)

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- The Arabian leopard lives in rocky mountains. Hunting, and the loss of the wild animals it eats, have left fewer than
    about 200 in the wild.
  - Saudi Arabia is helping: leopard cubs are born in a breeding centre in Taif, with a plan to return leopards to a
    protected reserve near AlUla.
  - 10 February is the International Day of the Arabian Leopard, recognised by the United Nations.

card.label: Find out together
card.md: find out how Saudi Arabia protects the leopard, and the oryx too (mystery C5).

card.label: Safety
card.md: none.

mysteries.credit: Wikimedia Commons, shankar s. from Dubai, united arab emirates, CC BY 2.0

mysteries.find: Rub two sandstones together and watch the grains

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- Elephant Rock is a huge sandstone rock, about 50 metres tall, near AlUla.
  - Her hint asks who carved it: nobody did. Wind blowing sand, and water from rare rains, slowly wore away the softer
    parts of the rock over a very long time, and left the shape of an elephant with its trunk.
  - This slow wearing away is called erosion. It is still going on today, too slowly to see.

card.label: Find out together
card.md:
rub two pieces of sandstone (or two rough stones) together over dark paper and look at the
  grains that fall.

card.label: Safety
card.md: rub gently, outdoors or over paper, keeping the dust away from eyes. Wash hands afterwards.

mysteries.credit: Wikimedia Commons, Richard Mortel, CC BY 2.0

mysteries.find: Look at photos of Al-Wahbah crater and the harrats

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- Deep under the ground, rock is so hot that it melts. When it comes out of the ground it is called lava.
  - When lava cools, it hardens into a dark rock called basalt. That is why the lava fields of Saudi Arabia, the harrats
    (الحرّات), are black.
  - The last eruption near Madinah was in 1256, more than 750 years ago, and its lava stopped south of the city.
  - Al-Wahbah crater is about 2 kilometres wide. It was made by a huge burst of steam when hot melted rock met water
    underground.

card.label: Find out together
card.md: look at photos of Al-Wahbah crater and the harrats on a map.

card.label: Safety
card.md: none (on a visit, stay well back from crater edges).

mysteries.find: Press a shell into clay to make a "fossil"

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- Millions of years ago, shallow seas covered parts of Arabia.
  - When a fish died, it sank and was covered by mud. Over a very long time the mud pressed into rock, and minerals
    slowly took the place of the bones, keeping their shape: a fossil.
  - Later the sea went away, the land dried, and wind wore the rock down until the fossil appeared.
  - Fossils of sea shells and other sea creatures have been found in Saudi rocks, for example in the Tuwaiq mountains
    near Riyadh.

card.label: Find out together
card.md: press a shell into clay or play dough to make a "fossil" print.

card.label: Safety
card.md: clay or play dough only (plaster gets hot as it sets).

mysteries.line: ماءٌ على رمل، وماءٌ على طين
mysteries.find: Pour the same water on both and time it (predict first)
mysteries.homeTip: sand and clay soil in two funnels

card.label: Explanation
card.md:
- Sand has big grains with big gaps between them, so water runs straight through and does not stay.
  - Clay has tiny grains packed close together, with tiny gaps, so water passes very slowly and much of it stays.
  - Good garden soil is a mix, so it holds some water and lets the rest drain away.
  - Her hint about planting: in pure sand plants dry out fast; in pure clay their roots can sit in water.

card.label: Find out together
card.md:
pour the same amount of water onto sand and onto clay soil and time how long it takes to come
  through. She predicts first.

card.label: Safety
card.md: an adult cuts the plastic bottles for the funnels. Wash hands after handling soil.
